title: Fortune and misfortune
hookLine: misfortune is where fortune rests; fortune hides misfortune (Tao Te Ching 58)

lines: A WEEK OF THE SMALL AND SOFT.
cards: An old man lives near the frontier, and one morning his horse runs off across the border. The neighbors come by to say how sorry they are. He shrugs.
Who's to say this isn't good luck?

That story comes from a different Chinese book, and it's a fitting way to close a week of the small and the soft: seeing the small, the weeds in the fields, the well planted, the newborn's grip, the quiet knower, the sage who meddles less.
Today, chapter fifty-eight takes a soft stance toward luck itself.

teach.b: First, the hinge of the chapter. In the Chinese, misfortune is what fortune leans on, and fortune is where misfortune lies hidden.

James Legge renders it as two cries: misery, with happiness right beside it; happiness, with misery lurking underneath. Then he asks: "Who knows what either will come to in the end?" Second, the reason for asking.
There's no fixed rule here, the chapter says. What's correct turns strange, and what's good turns ominous. And it adds, a little wearily, that people have been confused about this for a long time.
Third, the rest of the frontier story, from the book called the Huainanzi.

teach.h: THE HORSE, THE LEG, THE WAR.
teach.b: The runaway horse comes back, bringing a fine horse with it. The neighbors cheer. Who's to say this isn't bad luck, the old man asks.
His son rides the new horse, falls, and breaks his leg. The neighbors grieve. Who's to say.
Then war comes, the young men are taken to fight, and the son, lame, stays home. Every turn of the wheel looks final while it's happening. None of them is.
Fourth, how to live inside that.
The sage, the chapter says, is square without cutting anyone, has edges without wounding, is straight without overreaching, and shines without dazzling.

teach.h: WHO KNOWS WHAT EITHER WILL COME TO?
teach.b: Hold your shape, but don't judge too fast. That might mean meeting a rejection letter, a canceled trip or a sudden windfall with the same steady question. Not a cheerful one.
An honest one: who can tell yet?

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching pair chapter fifty-eight with the frontier-horse story from the Huainanzi, as a teaching to hold judgments of good and bad luck loosely.

o: good and bad luck, each leaning on the other
a streak of bad luck that never ends
a lucky charm that keeps every loss away

games.q: you're the old man at the frontier. your son has just broken his leg falling from the new horse. the neighbors grieve. what do you say?
o: who's to say this isn't good luck?
I knew that horse was trouble.
games.why: he asks who's to say; when war comes and the young men are taken, his son, lame, stays home.

practice: Bring to mind one thing that went wrong, recently or long ago, like a job that didn't come through, a move you didn't want or a plan that fell apart, and hold it the way you'd hold an old photograph.
Don't force it into a blessing; it may have been plain loss, and that's allowed. Just ask, gently, what grew next to it, and let the question stay open for the rest of the sit.
